The evidence lower bound (ELBO) supplies an alternative objective when a [latent-variable]{.term key="latent-variable"} model has a marginal likelihood that is difficult to compute.
For fixed observed data, it is a scalar function of the model and variational parameters that bounds the log evidence from below.
It is a bound on a log probability or density, not a probability distribution or a reconstruction error alone.
For the conditional version, let $A$ be an observed example, $o$ fixed context, and $z$ a latent variable.
The model has prior $p(z\mid o)$, decoder $p_\theta(A\mid o,z)$, and [approximate posterior]{.term key="variational-distribution"} $q_\phi(z\mid A,o)$.

## Reconstruction and prior KL {#objective}

For compactness, write $q_A=q_\phi(z\mid A,o)$ and $p_o=p(z\mid o)$.
Assume the model evidence is positive, all distributions are normalised, and the displayed expectations and KL terms are well defined.
For a finite objective, $q_A$ must place no probability mass where the prior or the observed example's likelihood is zero, apart from sets of probability zero.
The negative conditional evidence lower bound has two terms:

$$
  R=\mathbb E_{q_A}[-\log p_\theta(A\mid o,z)],
$$

$$
  K=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_A\Vert p_o),
  \qquad J=R+K.
$$

The reconstruction term $R$ rewards assigning high conditional likelihood to the demonstrated actions.
The KL term $K$ penalises disagreement between the encoder's latent distribution and the prior.
It does not directly measure action accuracy.
Both terms are minimised together, rather than one guaranteeing the other. [VAE, Eq. (3)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3).

Writing $B$ for the ELBO, the bound is

$$
  B=-J\leq\log p_\theta(A\mid o).
$$

The right side is the conditional log evidence after [marginalising]{.term key="marginalisation"} $z$.
Maximising $B$ is equivalent to minimising $J$.

## Deriving the bound {#deriving-the-bound}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: why reconstruction and KL form a bound"}

With $o$ fixed, marginalising the latent variable gives

$$
  p_\theta(A\mid o)
  =\int p_\theta(A\mid o,z)p_o(z)\,dz.
$$

Assume the relevant densities and expectations exist and the variational distribution has suitable support.
Introduce $q_A$ and apply [Jensen's inequality](expectations.qmd#jensen) to the concave logarithm:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \log p_\theta(A\mid o)&\geq B,\\
  B&=\mathbb E_{q_A}[\log p_\theta(A\mid o,z)]\\
  &\quad-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_A\Vert p_o).
  \end{aligned}
$$

Here, $B$ is the ELBO.
Negating it produces $R+K$, which training minimises.
The bound's gap is the KL divergence from $q_A$ to the true posterior, rather than the KL divergence to the prior. [VAE, Eqs. (1)–(3)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3).

:::

## The posterior approximation gap {#posterior-gap}

For an unconditional [VAE](../machine-learning/autoencoders.qmd#vae) observing $x$, the exact decomposition is:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \ln p_\theta(x)
  &=\operatorname{ELBO}(\theta,\phi;x)\\
  &\quad+D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_\phi(z\mid x)\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x)\right).
  \end{aligned}
$$

For fixed $\theta$, maximising the ELBO over $\phi$ minimises this posterior approximation gap.
When $\theta$ changes too, both the evidence and the true posterior change.
An increase in the ELBO alone therefore does not prove that this KL gap decreased.

## Reading the objective during training {#example}

Suppose two parameter settings give reconstruction and prior-KL terms $(R,K)=(8,1)$ and $(7,3)$ for the same example.
The second setting improves reconstruction, but $J$ increases from $9$ to $10$, so its ELBO decreases from $-9$ to $-10$.
A reconstruction improvement alone therefore need not improve the training objective.
The numerical comparison uses the unweighted objective $J=R+K$; changing the KL weight changes that tradeoff.

Likewise, the prior KL used in $J$ and the posterior KL measuring the bound's gap compare different pairs of distributions.
A small prior KL does not establish that the variational posterior is close to the true posterior.
If the variational distribution equals the true posterior, the posterior gap is zero and the ELBO equals the log evidence.
Computational usefulness additionally depends on being able to evaluate or estimate the objective and its gradients, as explained by [Monte Carlo estimation](expectations.qmd#latent-expectation) and [reparameterisation](reparameterization.qmd).
